title: Project Overview
description: Start with the README to understand what this project does: it turns the free Microsoft Copilot chat into an OpenAI-compatible API you can call from code. It works both as a Python library (CopilotClient) and a local server at localhost:8000/v1 that speaks the OpenAI format, so the official openai SDK works as a drop-in replacement.

title: Server Entry Point
description: app.py is the top-level script that launches the server. It imports server/__init__.py, which wires up uvicorn on a configurable host/port and ensures a Copilot auth session exists before serving requests. This is where the application transitions from a Python module into a running HTTP service.

title: API Router & Handlers
description: server/api.py is the heart of the OpenAI-compatible server — a FastAPI application with routes for listing models and generating chat completions. The chat_completions handler validates requests, enforces rate limits, then dispatches to either a streaming generator or a non-streaming completion builder. This file ties together all the server submodules.

title: OpenAI Format Translation
description: Building on the API router, these three modules handle the protocol translation. server/schemas.py defines Pydantic models for OpenAI's chat completion request shape. server/openai_format.py builds OpenAI-compliant response dicts and SSE streaming chunks. server/prompt.py flattens the OpenAI messages array (system messages, multi-turn history, content parts) into the single prompt string Copilot expects.

title: Rate Limiting & Configuration
description: server/ratelimit.py implements a token-bucket rate limiter that enforces a self-imposed ceiling on upstream requests to Microsoft Copilot. server/config.py reads environment variables for the model name, rate limit RPM, and burst size, providing sensible defaults. Together they protect both the upstream service and the local server from overload.

title: Copilot Client SDK
description: The copilot package barrel (copilot/__init__.py) re-exports the public API. The main class, CopilotClient in copilot/client.py, provides high-level chat() and stream() methods that abstract away authentication, Cloudflare clearance recovery, and conversation management. This is what the API server calls internally and what Python library users import directly.

title: Protocol Driver & Challenge Solving
description: copilot/driver.py implements the pure-HTTP Copilot provider over a Cloudflare-impersonating curl_cffi session. It handles conversation creation, attachment upload, WebSocket handshake, and streaming response parsing. copilot/protocol.py stores the WebSocket URL, handshake frames, and consent constants captured from a live session. copilot/challenges.py solves the hashcash and arithmetic proof-of-work challenges Microsoft requires before allowing chat.

title: Authentication & Browser Automation
description: copilot/auth.py manages signed-in session caching: it stores cookies and MSAL access tokens from a browser profile, and refreshes them automatically when they expire. copilot/browser.py drives Playwright for interactive sign-in, headless Cloudflare Turnstile clearance via WebSocket intercept, and chat token capture. Together they keep the session alive without user intervention.

title: Shared Data Models & Utilities
description: copilot/models.py defines the data types shared across both the pure-HTTP and browser paths: ImageResponse, the AbstractProvider base class, and the thread-safe Conversation container. copilot/utils.py provides low-level helpers — HTTP status checking, WebSocket JSON frame reassembly via drain_json, and image encoding utilities for attachment upload.

title: Containerization & Deployment
description: The Dockerfile packages the application based on the Playwright Python image (which ships Chromium preinstalled), installs dependencies, and serves the API on port 8000. docker-compose.yml adds port mapping, rate-limit environment variables, and a bind-mounted session volume for persistent browser profile storage across restarts, making it trivial to deploy anywhere Docker runs.
